title: Chapter 33 — The Specksnyder
paragraphs: Concerning the officers of the whale ship, this seems as good a place as any to describe a small domestic peculiarity on board, arising from the existence of the harpooner class of officers — a class unknown, of course, in any other service but the whale fleet.

The great importance attached to the harpooner's profession is shown by the fact that originally, in the old Dutch Fishery two centuries and more ago, command of a whale ship was not entirely in the hands of the person now called the captain. It was divided between him and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally, this word means Fat-Cutter, though in time it came to mean Chief Harpooner. In those days, the captain's authority was limited to navigation and the general management of the vessel, while over the whale-hunting department and everything related to it, the Specksnyder or Chief Harpooner reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch post still exists, but with much reduced authority. At present he ranks simply as senior harpooner and is merely one of the captain's lesser subordinates. Nevertheless, since the success of a whaling voyage largely depends on the harpooners' performance, and since in the American Fishery the harpooner is not only an important officer in the boat but also, under certain circumstances like night watches on a whaling ground, has command of the ship's deck — the grand political principle of the sea demands that he should nominally live apart from the men before the mast and be in some way distinguished as their professional superior, though they always familiarly regard him as their social equal.

Now, the key distinction between officer and ordinary seaman at sea is this: the officer lives aft, the seaman lives forward. Hence, on whale ships and merchant vessels alike, the mates have their quarters with the captain. And on most American whalers, the harpooners are also housed in the aft part of the ship — meaning they eat their meals in the captain's cabin and sleep in a space that connects with it indirectly.

Though the long duration of a Southern whaling voyage (by far the longest of all voyages now or ever made by man), its peculiar perils, and the community of interest among a company all of whom, high or low, depend for their profits not on fixed wages but on their common luck, together with their common vigilance, courage, and hard work — though all these things do in some cases tend to produce a less rigorous discipline than on merchant ships generally, still, no matter how much like an old Mesopotamian family these whalemen may, in some primitive instances, live together, the punctilious externals of the quarter-deck, at least, are seldom materially relaxed, and in no instance done away with. Indeed, there are many Nantucket ships on which you will see the skipper parading his quarter-deck with an elated grandeur not surpassed in any military navy — no, extorting almost as much outward homage as if he wore the imperial purple, and not the shabbiest of pilot-cloth.

And although of all men the moody captain of the Pequod was the least inclined to that shallowest kind of pretension; and although the only homage he ever demanded was total, instant obedience; although he required nobody to take the shoes off his feet before stepping onto the quarter-deck; and although there were times when, because of peculiar circumstances connected with events to be described later, he addressed them in unusual terms, whether condescending, or in terrorem (meant to intimidate), or otherwise; still, even Captain Ahab was far from ignoring the paramount forms and customs of the sea.

Nor, perhaps, will it fail to be noticed in the end that behind those forms and customs, as it were, he sometimes masked himself, incidentally using them for other and more private ends than they were legitimately meant to serve. That certain sultanism of his brain, which had otherwise remained to a good degree unmanifested — through those forms that same sultanism became incarnate in an irresistible dictatorship. For whatever a man's intellectual superiority may be, it can never take on a practical, usable supremacy over other men without the help of some sort of external arts and entrenchments, which are always in themselves more or less paltry and base. It is this that forever keeps God's true princes of the Empire from the world's hustings, the platforms of public election, and leaves the highest honors that this air can give to those men who become famous more through their infinite inferiority to the choice hidden handful of the Divine Inert than through their undoubted superiority over the dead level of the mass. Such great virtue lurks in these small things, when extreme political superstitions invest them, that in some royal instances they have given potency even to idiot imbecility. But when, as in the case of Nicholas the Czar, the ringed crown of geographical empire encircles an imperial brain, then the plebeian herds crouch abased before the tremendous centralization. Nor will the tragic dramatist who would depict mortal indomitableness in its fullest sweep and direct swing ever forget a hint so incidentally important to his art as the one just alluded to.

But Ahab, my Captain, still moves before me in all his Nantucket grimness and shagginess; and in this episode touching on emperors and kings, I must not conceal that I have to do only with a poor old whale-hunter like him; and therefore all outward majestic trappings and housings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! Whatever is to be grand in you must be plucked from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and given features in the unbodied air!
